article.body:
“Uh, it’s a senator of New York, Ma.” My voice was still shaky.

“Sruli Mendelsohn, how many times do I have to tell you not to make jokes at your mother’s expen— ” her voice trailed off as she got closer to the door.

“Mommy, meet the Senator.” Her expression was priceless.

“Mr. Senator,” my mother nervously began, “if this is about those unpaid parking tickets, believe me, I’ve been asking my husband to pay them for weeks—”

He smiled. “That’s very funny, but no, I’m here to meet the boy who gave our city a glow.” I felt my cheeks starting to blush.

My mother set the table with cake, and a choice of tea or coffee as the Senator and I sat face to face. “I had to postpone a meeting at City Hall to be here so I don’t have much time,” he began. “Sruli, I first heard about you when your friend, Rafi Adler, passed away. I was sorry to hear about the loss. I read about the large sum of money that Mr. Adler left for you, and how you intended to use it. I was impressed that a boy your age can be so selfless and caring for others. Still, as Senator, I couldn’t make time to visit you on that merit alone. But now that you’ve managed to unite this city with your Glow Campaign—brilliant idea, by the way—I had to thank you in person. As Senator of this diverse city, my ways of thanking you are very limited. As a Jew, however, I’m able to thank you by perhaps asking for your help.”

“Mr. Senator, I’m honored, but how can I possibly help you?”

“Well, Jewish education is something that is very near and dear to my heart. I believe that it is the Torah that keeps us close with Hashem. The thing is, many Jews don’t have much more than the Bible in their homes— if that! That’s how I grew up. I wasn’t taught much. But I want to give other Jewish kids a chance. If I donate money to your organization, can you call upon your soldiers to set up book fairs all over the

city, and maybe even all over the world, like you did with the “Got Glow?” campaign? That way, we can make Jewish books available at

reduced prices. The president of Barnes and Nobles is a close friend of mine. Maybe I can get him to host the book fairs in his stores across the country.”

“Well, Mr. Senator, you might not believe this, but your timing couldn’t be better. In just a few weeks, we celebrate the Yom Tov of Hey Teves, the day that we finally got ownership of the Previous Rebbe’s holy books. This day marks the victory we had after a long battle in court. The Rebbe would always stress that every Jewish family should have a house filled with books, and in celebration of Hey Teves, the Rebbe instructed all of us to buy more books of Chassidus for our homes. Maybe we can plan to have these Jewish book fairs on Hey Teves of this year!”

Just then, there was a knock at the door. It was the Senator’s driver.

“Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Senator, but we just got a ticket for double parking.”

“Y’gotta love this city,” the Senator laughed. “That’s okay, I should really get going. Sruli, I think it’s a great idea to have the book fairs on that holiday. Here’s a check to cover the expenses—and then some extra.”

As the limo took off, I unfolded the check. $500,000 was scribbled on the amount line. Here we go again, Boruch Hashem.

The next day after yeshiva— YES, YESHIVA COMES FIRST— I met with the head of Tzivos Hashem, and here’s what we came up with:

CAMPAIGN NAME: Jewish Book Day–The day Jewish homes wait for all year round @ your local Barnes and Noble.

ALSO ADVERTISED: Bring in any worn out Jewish book, and we’ll repair it, free of charge.

We emailed the poster to the senator’s office. Later that night, we got a reply from his secretary: “Sruli, Senator Goldberg loves your poster. Also, the President of Barnes and Noble jumped at the idea of having a Jewish Book Day in his stores, and asked for your permission to email the flier out to their global customer email list. Finally, Barnes and Noble would like to feature the Jewish books on their website on the day of the fair. Who can I direct them to? Best, Linzy at the Senator’s office.”

We put them in touch with Kehot Publication Society, and everything was arranged. Chassidishe books for children and adults were shipped across the world to the stores, and Barnes and Noble updated their website. Chayolim everywhere were called in to their Tzivos Hashem bases to prepare for the big day.

On Hey Teves, thousands of chayolim were deployed to Barnes and Noble stores across the globe. They spoke to customers about the importance of a Jewish home being full of holy books. Other skilled chayolim worked on

binding worn out copies of the English Tanach and other such books brought in by customers.

As a bonus for their hard work, each participating Chayol got to choose $100 worth of books to take home. Wanna know the really cool part? Since millions of Jewish books were ordered online that day, Barnes and Noble decided to keep the seforim on their website all year round.

Hey Teves was almost over, and I was in the store finishing up a conversation with an elderly woman named Esther. Just then, the store manager tapped me on the shoulder.
